newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian government closes ranks around top aide.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian government closes ranks around top aide.

text.p: The Peruvian government closed ranks on Friday around its shadowy security adviser, Vladimiro Montesinos, under pressure since a captured drug lord accused him of protecting traffickers.
In an overnight congressional hearing that lasted nearly 12 hours, the defence, interior and prime ministers all strenuously defended Montesinos.
"He has had an important role in the struggle against drug trafficking," Interior Minister Juan Briones Davila said.

"Montesinos drew up a series of laws which paved the way for the war against subversion which culminated in the capture of Abimael Guzman, leader of the Shining Path (guerrillas), a group which, together with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement, left more than 25,000 victims and $30 million in material damage," Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi said.

Opposition legislators denounced the ministers' speeches as a coverup of the accusations against Montesinos, who is seldom seen in public but is widely regarded as President Alberto Fujimori's right-hand man.
"The ministers have only told us half-truths," opposition legislator Henry Pease said during the debate.

Montesinos, a lawyer and legal adviser at the National Intelligence Service (SIN), was accused by confessed drug-trafficker Demetrio Chavez last month of accepting $50,000 a month in 1991 to protect activities in Peru's drug heartland, the Upper Huallaga Valley.

Local media and opposition legislators have leveled a variety of other accusations at him, from working for the U.S. CIA to using threats and tapping telephones to maintain his grip on the state security apparatus.
Montesinos has so far remained silent, ignoring a recommendation by Fujimori that he defend himself publicly.

Chavez recently retracted his accusation against Montesinos, saying he had been "confused." But his change of mind brought immediate claims in the media that intelligence officers had gotten to him in prison.
Opinon polls show that more than 90 percent of Peruvians are unconvinced by the government's defence of Montesinos and want a full investigation of the charges.
